title: Kindness Missions
tagline: Spot · Count · Go first · Offer · Keep
goal: Your kid finds out that kindness in public often comes down to going first. On real outings they spot small chances to help, count how many people saw the same chance and walked on, practise moving within about five seconds, and keep the moves that become habits.
need: Everyday public places: the bus, the store, a busy street or market
A notebook for the walk-past tally
Two weeks, a few outings at a time

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: In public, stay close and stay quiet. Younger kids always act with you right there, the offers stay small, and nobody approaches a stranger alone. Let them do the moving and the talking, then say exactly what you saw.

plan.what: Spot the chances and count who walked past (Steps 1 and 2).
Practise going first, then make real offers (Steps 3 and 4).

plan.when: At home, then two weeks later
plan.what: Talk it through and check the habit (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: They freeze and the moment passes
troubleshoot.a: That's the 'someone else will' feeling from the inside. Say nothing in the moment. Later, ask what stopped them, and pick the next chance together, like the next door you reach.

troubleshoot.q: They're too shy to talk to strangers
troubleshoot.a: Start with go-firsts that need no words: holding a door, or handing back something dropped. Offer lines can wait until moving first feels easy.

troubleshoot.q: A no thanks put them off
troubleshoot.a: A no thanks is someone choosing for themselves, not a failed mission. They still went first, and that's the part that counts.

lesson.text: When lots of people see someone who needs a hand, each one tends to wait for somebody else. Psychologists call it the bystander effect. Kindness often just means going first. The missions are practice for those five seconds.
lesson.before: 'Someone else will give him their seat.'

model.line: An older man standing on a full city bus.
Everyone sitting nearby could see him there.
'Someone else will' kept them all in their seats.
He stood up and offered his seat.

lesson.modelNote: Every seat on that bus had the same thought, so nobody moved. He didn't wait to see who would, and the whole thing took a few seconds.

steps.title: Spot the chances
steps.why: Most chances to help in public last a few seconds. Kids who look for them start seeing them everywhere.
steps.kid: On one outing, like a bus ride, a market or a busy street, your kid looks for small chances to help, using the Where to look card in the Kindness Toolkit at the end of the guide. They note each one: who it was, and what would have helped.
steps.you: Walk slowly, and point out one chance quietly to get them started: 'Full hands at that door.' Then let them do the spotting.
ask: What did that person need right then?
Which chance was over the fastest?
steps.tip: Doors, stairs, bus seats and checkout lines are where most small chances happen.

levels.explore: Spot one person who could use a hand, and whisper it to a parent.
levels.develop: Write down every chance you spot in 20 minutes, and what would have helped.
levels.extend: Note where each chance happened, and find the spot on your usual route with the most.

steps.title: Count who walked past
steps.why: This is the surprise. When lots of people see the same chance, each one tends to wait for someone else.
steps.kid: For each chance, your kid counts how many people saw it and walked on before anyone helped, using the Walk-past tally card. They tally it in the notebook, and note whether somebody went first in the end, or nobody did.
steps.you: Keep it curious, not judging. Nobody walking past is a bad person. Ask what each one might have been telling themselves.
ask: How many people saw it before someone helped?
What do you think they were telling themselves?
steps.tip: Count only people who clearly looked. Someone on their phone may never have seen it.

levels.explore: Hold up a finger for each person who walks past, and count them together.
levels.develop: Tally walk-pasts for every chance on one outing, and work out the average.
levels.extend: Compare a busy place with a quiet one, and see if a bigger crowd means a longer wait before someone helps.

steps.title: Go first in five seconds
steps.why: Waiting is how the moment passes. A move they've practised can happen before 'someone else will' kicks in.
steps.kid: At home, your kid practises the Five-second move: you drop a glove or carry too much, and they spot it, count in their head and move before five. Then they try it for real on an outing, with you nearby, using the Go first safely card.
steps.you: Play the person who needs a hand a few times, in different ways. In public, stay close enough to step in, and let them be the one who moves.
ask: What did you do in the first second?
What made you wait, if you did?
steps.tip: Holding a door or handing back something dropped needs no words. Those make the easiest first go.

levels.explore: Practise with a parent at home, then hold one door in public with a parent beside you.
levels.develop: Go first on three real chances this week, within about five seconds.
levels.extend: Write the exact thought that makes you wait, then the line you'll answer it with next time.

steps.title: Make the offer
steps.why: An offer leaves the choice with the other person. Going first is about offering, not about getting a yes.
steps.kid: When a chance needs words, your kid uses a line from the Offer and answer card, like 'Would you like a hand with that?' Then they accept whatever comes back: a yes, a no thanks or a shrug. They log each go-first and each answer.
steps.you: Stand back and let them speak for themselves. If they get a no thanks, catch their eye and smile. They did it right.
ask: What did you say, word for word?
How did the no thanks feel?
steps.tip: Offer, don't grab. Picking up someone's bag without asking can frighten them.

levels.explore: Say one offer line with a parent beside you, like 'Would you like to go ahead?' in a line.
levels.develop: Make three offers this week, and log each answer.
levels.extend: After a no thanks, guess why that person might prefer to manage on their own, and what it tells you about offering.

steps.title: Talk it through and keep it
steps.why: A few go-firsts are practice. The ones still happening two weeks later, without thinking, are the habit.
steps.kid: At home, your kid looks back through the notebook and picks what was hardest: going first, offering or hearing a no. Two weeks later, they use the Habit check card to sort which moves now happen without thinking and which still need practice.
steps.you: Share your own hardest part first. At the habit check, name one move you've seen them do with no reminder.
ask: Which was hardest: going first, offering or hearing a no?
Which move do you do now without thinking?
steps.tip: Hook one move to something you already do, like every time you reach a door or step onto a bus.

levels.explore: Tell a parent the hardest part, and pick one move to keep doing.
levels.develop: Name your hardest part, and plan an easier go-first to practise it.
levels.extend: Teach the Five-second move to someone at home, and see if they go first on your next outing.

conclusion.headline: They move first while others wait.
conclusion.text: Say nothing on your next bus ride or at the next busy door, and see who moves. If your kid is up and offering before you've even spotted the chance, those five seconds belong to them now.
conclusion.celebrate: When they go first with no reminder, say: 'Three people walked past that, and you didn't wait. You went first.'
extensions: Find out why first aid courses teach you to point at one person and say 'You, call for help'
Notice when someone goes first for you this week, and thank them
Ask a grandparent about a time a stranger went first for them, and what they still remember
Go first at home too: be the first to say sorry, or the first to start the dishes

signs: They get up for someone before anyone asks
They notice when a crowd is waiting for someone else
They take a no thanks with a smile
makeItReal: On your next bus ride or trip to the store, look for one small chance together and count the people who walk past it. Then let your kid be the one who goes first.

fromHome.text: Coming home on the city bus, my son gave his seat to an older man. The man thanked him, and told him he doesn't see many young people being so kind these days. When my son was about to get off, the man gave him $5 for his kindness.
